meta.title: Who really said "Habit is habit, and not to be flung out of the window by any man, but coaxed down-stairs a step at a time"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Twain really wrote it — as a Pudd'nhead Wilson's Calendar epigraph in The Tragedy of Pudd'nhead Wilson (1894). The "tossed out the window" version is not his.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Habit is habit, and not to be flung out of the window by any man, but coaxed down-stairs a step at a time'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Twain: an 1894 Pudd'nhead Wilson's Calendar epigraph, verified in the book text. But the popular 'tossed out the window' rewording is a later corruption.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Twain wrote it, and the wording checks out. It stands as the second of two “Pudd’nhead Wilson’s Calendar” epigraphs heading Chapter VI, “Swimming in Glory,” of The Tragedy of Pudd’nhead Wilson (1894) — and he liked it enough to use it again, in the narrator’s voice, in Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc.

source.heading: The source, on the page

docMeta.dd: Serialized in The Century Magazine, 1893–1894; book edition, American Publishing Company, Hartford, 1894

source.excerpt:
CHAPTER VI. Swimming in Glory.

Let us endeavor so to live that when we come to die even the undertaker will be sorry.—Pudd’nhead Wilson’s Calendar.

Habit is habit, and not to be flung out of the window by any man, but coaxed down-stairs a step at a time.—Pudd’nhead Wilson’s Calendar.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ finds no instance before Twain and dates the earliest to the January 1894 installment of the serialized Pudd’nhead Wilson in The Century Magazine (vol. 47, no. 3), quote page 334.

The book text confirms it: Project Gutenberg’s transcription ↗ of the 1894 American Publishing Company edition prints the sentence as the second Calendar epigraph under “CHAPTER VI. Swimming in Glory.”

An independent scan agrees — the page text of an 1897 American Publishing Company printing at the Internet Archive ↗ carries the same wording, hyphen and all, followed by the Calendar attribution line.

Twain used it a second time: the sentence appears inside the narration of Book I, chapter 6 of Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc ↗, which QI cites to Harper’s New Monthly Magazine, May 1895, page 849.
source.excerptNote: Chapter VI opens with two Calendar entries; the habit line is the second. Transcription as printed in the 1894 text.

source.rightsNote: The Tragedy of Pudd’nhead Wilson was first published in 1893–1894 — serially in The Century Magazine, then as a book from the American Publishing Company in 1894 — far earlier than the 1931 US copyright cutoff, so the text is in the public domain. The original 1894 copyright was registered to Olivia L. Clemens and to the Century Company for the serial; both expired long ago.

author.name: Mark Twain
author.heading: Who was Mark Twain?
author.bio: Samuel Langhorne Clemens wrote as Mark Twain, a riverboat pilot’s call turned into the most recognisable byline in American letters. The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876) and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884) made him famous; the aphorism made him quotable, and he sharpened one-liners with the same care he gave a chapter. That gift is exactly why he is now the internet’s most magnetic false attribution — but this particular line really is his, in print, and easy to check.

misattribution.heading: The line is Twain’s. Most versions of it are not.
misattribution.intro: This is the rarer case: a genuine Twain sentence that still gets quoted wrong almost everywhere. Within two years of publication the verb had already been swapped, and each rewriting bred more. Quote Investigator’s verdict is narrow and worth honouring — Twain earns credit for the version with “flung,” and only that one.

items.why: “A bad habit cannot be tossed out the window; it must be coaxed down the stairs a step at a time” ran under Twain’s name in Coronet in 1948; Reader’s Digest reprinted a near-identical “tossed” version in 1958, dropping the word “bad,” and from there it passed into the quotation books. Twain never wrote “tossed” — Quote Investigator traces the drift ↗.

Mabel Thatcher Wellman’s 1896 article in Education gave it as “No man is strong enough to throw habit out of the window, it must be coaxed step by step down stairs”; Ellen H. Richards printed another “throw” variant in 1900, and John Harvey Kellogg in 1915 had habits that “cannot be taken by the heels and neck and thrown down stairs, but must be coaxed down, a step at a time.” All are reconstructions from memory ↗, not Twain’s text.

items.who: Twain, cited to nothing at all
items.why: The line usually circulates as a bare “— Mark Twain,” which is exactly why readers get suspicious: the enquiry that prompted QI’s investigation ↗ came from someone who could find no solid citation behind the popular wording. The real citation is a chapter epigraph, and it is easy to check.

misattribution.truthLine: Twain wrote it — with flung, and coaxed down-stairs a step at a time — as a “Pudd’nhead Wilson’s Calendar” epigraph to Chapter VI of The Tragedy of Pudd’nhead Wilson (1894) ↗, and used it a second time in Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc.

context.heading: Why a calendar wrote Twain’s best lines
lead: The Tragedy of Pudd’nhead Wilson is a courtroom novel about switched babies and fingerprints, but the thing readers actually carried away was the furniture: every chapter opens with an entry from “Pudd’nhead Wilson’s Calendar,” a fictional almanac kept by the town’s resident misunderstood genius. It let Twain publish a book of aphorisms inside a novel without anyone calling it a book of aphorisms.

Chapter VI gets two of them, back to back — the undertaker joke, then the habit line. Put together they are the whole Twain method in eight inches of type: a gag about dying well, then a genuinely useful piece of advice about self-improvement, delivered as a physical comedy of a man wrestling something heavy toward a staircase. It is not “quit your bad habits.” It is a description of how quitting actually feels.
detailsBody: He reused it, which is the strongest internal evidence that he rated it. A year later, in Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc, the narrator — Joan’s page and secretary — resolves to stop lying to her, and then immediately opens with a small lie anyway, “for habit is habit, and not to be flung out of the window by any man, but coaxed downstairs a step at a time.” The aphorism becomes a joke at the narrator’s own expense.

Note the drift in that one word across printings: “down-stairs” in the 1894 Calendar epigraph, “down stairs” in the 1895 Harper’s serialization of Joan of Arc, and “downstairs” in the Gutenberg text of the book. That tiny instability is the crack the later rewritings widened.
context.pull: Twain slipped a book of aphorisms inside a novel and let a fictional almanac take the credit.
